# Disclosure Gate

A build step that must pass before anything derived from sensitive input may be published. It turns
"I anonymised it" from an assertion into a check that can fail.

> "Anonymization you can't verify is a liability."
> — labour-fraud-analysis-a-forensic-data-investigation/docs/methodology.md, 2026-07-11

> "the claim \"no PII here\" is not a promise, it's a **passing test** — and it caught real leaks
> during development"
> — labour-fraud-analysis-a-forensic-data-investigation/docs/methodology.md, 2026-07-11

## The four checks

`validate_anonymization.py` in [[labour-fraud-analysis]] runs, and must print a PASS:

1. **Leak scan.** A blocklist is assembled **at run time** from the private source — every sensitive
   column across people, companies, worksites, issuing authorities, permits and residence documents —
   and grepped across the data, docs, viewer and notebook directories. The blocklist is never written
   to disk.
2. **Stem guard.** Word stems from a git-ignored local rules module, catching inflected and truncated
   forms that an exact-string blocklist misses.
3. **Regex sweep.** Shape-based patterns for phone numbers and national identity numbers, plus an
   email pattern that allow-lists the fictional inboxes and domains the generated world is supposed to
   contain.
4. **Structural integrity.** Primary-key uniqueness and foreign-key closure across ten tables — because
   an anonymisation run that silently dropped or duplicated rows has damaged the dataset even if it
   leaked nothing. See [[third-normal-form]].

One implementation detail is worth stealing: notebooks are scanned by **cell source only**.

> "For notebooks, scan only cell SOURCE (code+markdown), never base64 output blobs — random base64
> would trip the substring checks."
> — labour-fraud-analysis-a-forensic-data-investigation/src/validate_anonymization.py, 2026-07-11

A gate that cries wolf gets disabled. Excluding the one input class guaranteed to produce false
positives is what keeps it enabled.

## The finding: the CI claim is overstated

`confidence: high`, interview-confirmed 2026-07-28.

The README states that no value in the dataset identifies a real party — "a claim that is
test-verified in CI". **It is not, on a clean runner.** Checks 1 and 2 both require the private source
and the git-ignored rules module, neither of which exists on a public runner, and the workflow says so
itself:

> "On a clean runner the private source + rules are absent, so the leak/stem scans skip and this
> enforces structural integrity + the PII regex sweep."
> — labour-fraud-analysis-a-forensic-data-investigation/.github/workflows/ci.yml, 2026-07-11

So public CI enforces **checks 3 and 4 only**. The strong checks run on one machine, on demand, by
one person. That is not nothing — it is how the real leaks were caught during development — but it is
weaker than the README claims, and it is the single largest prose-vs-artifact gap in the repository.
See [[documentation-drift]]. A milder instance sits alongside it: the README and methodology call this
a "four-way" gate while the validator's own docstring says "two independent checks".

This asymmetry is a general property of secret-scanning gates, not a local mistake: **the check that
needs the secret cannot run where the secret is absent.** Any project whose gate depends on private
input should state which subset a public runner actually enforces.

## Related discipline

The gate is the privacy analogue of [[verify-the-load-dont-declare-it]] — replace a claim with a
query that can fail — and it is wired into [[make]] and [[github-actions]] so that it is not optional.
